title: For the Sake of My Name: Israel's History Retold
summary: When elders come to consult the LORD, he refuses them and has Ezekiel recount Israel's history as a story of rebellion from Egypt to the present, in which God repeatedly held back his wrath only for the sake of his name. He then promises a new exodus: he will gather his people, judge them in the wilderness of the nations, purge the rebels, and bring the rest home to worship him on his holy mountain. A short oracle of fire against the forest of the south closes the chapter.
story: Chapter 20 opens the third dated section of the book and falls roughly midway between Ezekiel's call and the fall of Jerusalem. The elders who sit before him (compare 8:1 and 14:1) want a word from God, probably a word of hope. Instead they get a history lesson that reaches back past Manasseh and past the judges to Egypt itself. Chapter 16 told Israel's story as a marriage betrayed; chapter 20 tells it without metaphor, as a pattern of rebellion and restraint. The chapter also points forward. Its promise of a second exodus through the wilderness and back to the land anticipates the restoration oracles of chapters 34 to 37 and the vision of a renewed temple on a high mountain in chapters 40 to 48.
historical:
The date in verse 1, the tenth day of the fifth month of the seventh year of Jehoiachin's exile, falls in the summer of 591 BC, about five years before Jerusalem's fall. In Jerusalem, Zedekiah reigned as Babylon's vassal and was drifting toward rebellion, encouraged by the hope of Egyptian help. The exiles in Babylon were watching and hoping for a quick return.

The practices the chapter condemns are well attested in Judah's last century. Worship at high places, hilltop shrines with altars and sacred trees, persisted despite the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah (2 Kings 18:4; 23:8). Child sacrifice, passing sons and daughters through the fire, is charged against Kings Ahaz and Manasseh (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6) and was practiced at Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem until Josiah defiled it (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). Verse 32 voices a real temptation of exile: to settle down and serve the gods of the land where you now live, like every other displaced people.
cultural:
Inquiring of the LORD was a recognized practice. People brought questions to a prophet, as kings did with Elisha (2 Kings 3:11) and Zedekiah did with Jeremiah (Jeremiah 21:1-2), expecting a word from God in answer. For God to refuse to be consulted was itself a verdict. The oath with an uplifted hand (verses 5, 15, 23, 42) pictures the gesture of someone swearing a solemn vow, and the chapter uses it both for God's promise to bring Israel into the land and for his oaths of judgment.

The Sabbath carries unusual weight here. For exiles far from the temple, with no altar and no sacrifices, keeping the seventh day was one of the few public marks of belonging to the LORD. Ezekiel calls it a sign between God and Israel (verses 12 and 20, echoing Exodus 31:13), and profaning it appears in every stage of the history. Verse 29 contains a wordplay that is hard to bring into English: God asks what (mah) is this high place (bamah) to which you go (ba'im), as if mocking the very name of the shrine.
literary: Verses 5 to 26 follow a repeated cycle through three stages of history: Israel in Egypt, the first generation in the wilderness, and their children in the wilderness. Each time God reveals himself and gives his commands; Israel rebels; God resolves to pour out his wrath; then he holds back for the sake of his name, lest it be profaned among the nations. The repetition is deliberate and relentless. The cycle breaks in verses 27 to 31 with life in the land, where there is no holding back, only the question whether the present generation is any different. Verses 32 to 44 then reverse the pattern with a new exodus, in which the same strong hand and outstretched arm that brought Israel out of Egypt will now bring them out of the nations. The final oracle (verses 45 to 49) begins chapter 21 in Hebrew Bibles; the fire in the southern forest is explained in the next chapter as the sword against Jerusalem.

outline.t: Elders come to inquire; God refuses to be consulted
Rebellion in Egypt, restraint for the sake of God's name
Idolatry in the land and in the present generation
A new exodus: judgment in the wilderness of the nations
Restored worship on God's holy mountain
Fire in the forest of the south

doctrines.note: God acts for the sake of his name (verses 9, 14, 22, 44). He spares and restores Israel not because they deserve it but because his own character and reputation among the nations are at stake. Grace here is rooted in who God is, not in who Israel is.

The chapter traces idolatry back to Egypt and shows it clinging to Israel through every generation. Its most horrifying form, the sacrifice of children, reveals where the worship of other gods finally leads.

The promised restoration repeats the shape of the exodus: God brings his people out, judges and purifies them, and brings them home to worship him. Salvation is described as a new exodus, a pattern the rest of Scripture takes up.

words.note: Shem, name. In the Bible a name stands for a person's character and reputation. God's name being profaned among the nations means his reputation being dragged down by his people's behavior and by their destruction. The chapter's refrain is that God guards his name.
Shabbat, Sabbath, the seventh day of rest. It appears six times in this chapter as a sign between God and his people. Its profanation stands for Israel's refusal to belong to the LORD alone.

Darash, to seek or inquire. It frames the chapter: the elders come to inquire (verse 1), and God declares that he will not be inquired of by them (verses 3 and 31). The word can describe seeking God in worship or consulting him through a prophet.

Midbar, wilderness. The wilderness is where Israel first rebelled and where God disciplined them; in verse 35 it becomes the wilderness of the nations, where God will again meet his people face to face in judgment and cleansing before bringing them home.

christ: The new exodus Ezekiel promises in verses 33 to 44 is one of the patterns the New Testament uses to describe what God does in Christ. The Gospels set Jesus in the wilderness, tested forty days where Israel was tested forty years, and faithful where they were not (Matthew 4:1-11). In Luke's account of the transfiguration, Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about his departure, using the Greek word exodus, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The chapter's insistence that God saves for the sake of his name, not because of Israel's merit (verse 44), anticipates the New Testament's teaching that salvation is by grace. And the promise that God will accept his people as a pleasing aroma (verse 41) finds an echo in Paul's description of Christ giving himself up as a fragrant offering (Ephesians 5:2). These are connections of pattern and theme drawn by later writers, not predictions spelled out by Ezekiel.

hard.q: What does God mean when he says he gave Israel statutes that were not good (verses 25 and 26)?
hard.a: These verses are among the hardest in the prophets, because they seem to say that God gave laws that led to death, even to child sacrifice. Interpreters have offered several readings. Many read them as judicial handing over: because Israel rejected God's good laws, he gave them up to the destructive practices they preferred, much as Psalm 81:12 says God gave his people over to their stubborn hearts and as Paul says God gave people over to their desires (Romans 1:24). The BSB's translation, gave them over, reflects this reading. Others think Ezekiel is referring to Israel's twisted reading of a real law, the command to give the firstborn to the LORD (Exodus 22:29), which the law itself says must be redeemed for sons (Exodus 13:13; 34:20), but which some Israelites perverted into child sacrifice. A third reading takes the words as bitter irony, God speaking in the voice of the people's own claim that he demanded such things, which Jeremiah flatly denies (Jeremiah 7:31). What every reading agrees on is that the chapter condemns child sacrifice as the height of defilement and never presents it as something God desired.

questions: The elders came to consult God but were not ready to hear about their own history. When have you wanted guidance from God without wanting to be examined?
God repeatedly spared Israel for the sake of his name rather than their merit. How does it change your view of grace to see it grounded in God's character rather than your record?
Verse 32 voices the temptation to be like the nations. Where do you feel the pull to blend in with the gods of the culture around you?
